# Categorical and textual data {#sec-text}

::: {.content-hidden}
PLAN (Oct 2026)

Keep the book's probabilistic framing throughout: anomalies in categorical data have high surprisal -log p(x); anomalous documents have high surprisal under a language model, or low density in a feature space; authorship verification is a one-class problem (is this text surprising given the author's known work?).

1. Anomalies in categorical data
   - One variable: surprisal -log p(x); surprisal probability = sum of p over categories no more probable than the observed one.
     Handles many rare categories (each individually rare) and ties (discrete surprisal probabilities).
     Smoothing for unseen categories.
   - Several variables: the full joint table is sparse.
     Independence model (AVF-style scores); pairwise/conditional surprisals -log p(x_j \| x\_-j) for "common values, rare combination"; Chow-Liu trees / Bayesian networks as a pointer only.
   - Anomalous cells in a contingency table: standardised residuals from a log-linear independence model (a different question from anomalous rows; leads into CA).
   - Example: BITRE Australian Road Deaths Database (CC BY): state, road user, crash type, speed limit, day/time, age, remoteness.
     Also used in section 3.

2. Correspondence analysis
   - CA of a two-way table: row profiles, chi-squared distance, inertia.
     Anomalous rows are profiles far from the centroid / with large contribution to inertia.
     Biplot (link to ch9).
   - Example: wine country x variety (which countries have unusual variety profiles).
     CA, MCA and FAMD all via FactoMineR.
   - MCA for many categorical variables: numerical coordinates, then ch6/ch9 methods.
     Explains the CA step in HDoutliers.
   - NOTE: highdim.qmd (HDoutliers) already says "correspondence analysis" before this chapter defines it.
     Replace with a plain-words description plus a forward section reference.

3. Mixed numerical and categorical data
   - Factorise the density: f(y, x) = f(y \| x) p(x), so surprisals add; f(y \| x) from the ch8 regression machinery with categorical predictors.
   - Distance-based alternatives: Gower distance with kNN/LOF/stray (ch6); FAMD (FactoMineR) as the mixed-data analogue of PCA/MCA.
   - Examples: wine_reviews (price given points, variety, country), extending the ch1 Shiraz example; road deaths.

4. From text to numbers (brief)
   - Tokens, document-term matrix, tf-idf, function vs content words, using tidytext (Silge & Robinson, Text Mining with R).

5. Feature-based anomalies in text
   - Document features: length, type-token ratio, word and sentence length, punctuation, sentiment, readability, out-of-vocabulary share.
     Then HDR / stray / LOF on the feature matrix (parallels the ch13 features strategy).
   - Example: wine review descriptions.
     Needs the original `description` column (dropped by fetch_wine_reviews()) restored in the weird package, giving one data set with numerical, categorical and text variables.
     Natural target: reviews whose wording disagrees with their points.

6. Language-model surprisals
   - Unigram / n-gram models give each document a surprisal; perplexity = exp(mean surprisal).
     Show which words drive a document's score.
   - Topic models (LDA) for unusual topic mixtures; document embeddings + PCA (link to ch9).
   - Example: wine review descriptions (same data as section 5).
   - Discussion: detectors of machine-generated text (DetectGPT, Binoculars) flag text that is too predictable, i.e. unusually LOW surprisal.

7. Was this text written by someone else?
   - Stylometric features: frequencies of the most common function words (Mosteller & Wallace).
     Burrows' Delta is a Manhattan distance on standardised frequencies (link to ch6).
   - Authorship verification as one-class anomaly detection: split the author's known works into chunks, model the distribution of their feature vectors, score the questioned text, calibrate by leaving one chunk out.
     Brief mention of unmasking (Koppel & Schler, 2004) and the imposters method.
   - Example: The Royal Book of Oz (1921), credited to L Frank Baum but written by Ruth Plumly Thompson (Binongo, 2003, Chance).
     Gutenberg #30537; Baum's 14 Oz books and several later Thompson Oz books are also on Gutenberg (the latter as a check).

Out of scope: sequences of categorical events (log codes) belong in events.qmd.

Data for the weird package (book must not download from Gutenberg at build time; gutenbergr only in data-raw):

- road_deaths package data (BITRE ARDD, 1989-2025)
- `description` column restored in wine_reviews
- fetch_oz_books(): paragraphs of 29 Oz books (Baum 14, Thompson 15)

New book dependencies: tidytext (FactoMineR already installed).

```{r}
#| label: setup10
#| include: false
#| cache: false

source("before-each-chapter.R")
```

The methods in the previous chapters all assume numerical data, where values can be ordered, averaged, and compared by the distances between them.
Many data sets also contain **categorical variables**, which take one of a fixed set of values, called **categories** (or levels), such as gender, state, or country.
Categories usually have no natural order and there is no natural measure of distance between them.

Text is an extreme example of categorical data.
Each word comes from a vocabulary of many thousands of words, most of which are rarely used, and a document is a sequence of words whose meaning depends on their order.

The probabilistic approach of this book still applies to both kinds of data.
For categorical data, the density is replaced by a probability mass function, and an anomaly is an observation with a high surprisal (@sec-surprisals): a category, or a combination of categories, that rarely occurs.
For text, a document is anomalous if it is improbable under a model of the language in which it is written, or if its features have low density compared to those of other documents.

The chapter starts with anomalies in categorical data, including anomalous cells in tables of counts.
Correspondence analysis then converts categorical data to numerical coordinates, to which the methods of @sec-distance-methods and @sec-highdim can be applied, and the methods are then extended to data containing both numerical and categorical variables.
The rest of the chapter is about text: converting documents to numbers, finding anomalous documents from their features or from their surprisals under a language model, and finally deciding whether a text was written by the author to whom it is attributed.
That last question is also one of anomaly detection: is the text surprising, given the author's known work?

## Anomalies in categorical data {#sec-categorical}

The examples in this section use the Australian Road Deaths Database\ [@ARDD], compiled by the Bureau of Infrastructure and Transport Research Economics, which records every person killed in a road crash in Australia.
The `road_deaths` data set in the **`weird`** package contains the `r scales::comma(NROW(road_deaths))` deaths from January 1989 to December 2025.
Each row is one person killed, and the variables include the state or territory, the type of road user (driver, passenger, pedestrian, motorcycle rider, motorcycle pillion passenger or pedal cyclist), the person's age and sex, the type of road, and the speed limit where the crash occurred.
Most of the variables are categorical.

### One categorical variable

Suppose the observations $y_1,\dots,y_n$ each take one of $K$ categories $c_1,\dots,c_K$.
This is known as a **factor** variable, and the categories are its **levels**.
Let $f$ denote the probability mass function of the underlying random variable, so that $f(c_k)$ is the probability that an observation falls in category $c_k$, and the surprisal of $y_i$ is $s_i = -\log f(y_i)$, as in @eq-surprisal.
The integral in the surprisal probability (@eq-pi-density) becomes a sum over the categories:
$$
  p_i = \sum_{k=1}^K f(c_k)\, 𝟙\big(f(c_k) \le f(y_i)\big).
$$ {#eq-pi-categorical}
That is, $p_i$ is the total probability of all categories that are no more probable than the category of $y_i$.
In practice, $f(c_k)$ is estimated by $n_k/n$, the proportion of observations in category $c_k$.

Being rare is not enough to make a category anomalous.
If there are $K = 1000$ equally likely categories, then $f(y_i) = 0.001$ for every observation, but $p_i = 1$, because no category is more probable than any other.
A category is anomalous only when all the categories that are no more probable together account for a small proportion of the data.
This is the advantage of surprisal probabilities over the simpler rule of flagging any category whose proportion is below some threshold.

Because $p_i$ takes only a few distinct values, the false positive rate when observations with $p_i < \alpha$ are labelled anomalous is at most $\alpha$, rather than exactly $\alpha$ as it is for continuous data.
This is because the categories with $p_i < \alpha$ have total probability equal to the largest of their surprisal probabilities, which is itself less than $\alpha$.
Categories with the same probability are tied: they have the same surprisal and the same surprisal probability, which includes the probabilities of all the tied categories.

The type of road on which each crash occurred has been recorded since 2014, for `r scales::comma(sum(!is.na(road_deaths$road_type)))` deaths, using `r english::words(nlevels(road_deaths$road_type))` categories.
When applied to a factor, the `surprisals()` and `surprisals_prob()` functions estimate $f(c_k)$ by $n_k/n$, and return $s_i$ and $p_i$ for each observation.
All deaths on the same type of road have the same surprisal and surprisal probability, so `count()` reduces them to one row per road type.

```{r}
#| label: road-types
#| code-fold: false

road_types <- road_deaths |>
  filter(!is.na(road_type)) |>
  mutate(
    s = surprisals(road_type),
    p = surprisals_prob(road_type)
  ) |>
  count(road_type, s, p) |>
  arrange(p)
road_types
```

```{r}
#| label: road-types-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: road-types

road_type_p <- function(type) road_types$p[road_types$road_type == type]
busway <- road_deaths |> filter(road_type == "Busway")
thoroughfare <- road_deaths |> filter(road_type == "Pedestrian Thoroughfare")
# The prose describes the rarest road types and the flagged road types
stopifnot(
  min(road_deaths$year[!is.na(road_deaths$road_type)]) == 2014,
  nlevels(road_deaths$road_type) == 8,
  road_types$road_type[1] == "Busway",
  road_types$road_type[2] == "Pedestrian Thoroughfare",
  road_types$road_type[3] == "Access road",
  NROW(busway) == 2,
  all(busway$lga == "Brisbane"),
  all(busway$road_user == "Pedal cyclist"),
  NROW(thoroughfare) == 6,
  sum(thoroughfare$speed_limit >= 80) == 5,
  sum(road_types$p < 0.01) == 3,
  road_type_p("Collector Road") > 0.05
)
```

The least probable road type is a busway (a road reserved for buses), with two deaths, both of pedal cyclists in Brisbane, so its surprisal probability is $2/n =$ `r sprintf("%.5f", road_type_p("Busway"))`.
The six deaths on pedestrian thoroughfares have $p_i = 8/n =$ `r sprintf("%.5f", road_type_p("Pedestrian Thoroughfare"))`, which includes the two busway deaths.
Five of these six deaths occurred where the speed limit was 80 km/h or more, so some of them may have been given the wrong road type.
With $\alpha = 0.01$, access roads are also anomalous ($p_i =$ `r sprintf("%.4f", road_type_p("Access road"))`), so the three anomalous road types together account for `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * road_type_p("Access road"))`% of the deaths, less than $\alpha$.

Estimating $f(c_k)$ by $n_k/n$ causes problems for very rare categories.
A category with no observations has an estimated probability of zero, so a new observation in that category has an infinite surprisal.
The same happens to a category with a single observation when leave-one-out surprisals (@sec-loo-surprisals) are used, because the observation's own category is then empty.
A simple fix is to add a small constant $a$ to every count, giving $\hat{f}(c_k) = (n_k + a)/(n + Ka)$.
This is the posterior mean of $f(c_k)$ under a symmetric Dirichlet prior with parameter $a$ [@Agresti2013].
The usual choices are $a = 1$, a uniform prior (Laplace's rule of succession), and $a = 1/2$, the Jeffreys prior, which gives good predictions even for the rarest categories\ [@Krichevsky1981].
This requires the list of possible categories to be known in advance, and it reduces the surprisals of the rarest categories, so it matters most when $n$ is small compared to $K$.

In `surprisals()` and `surprisals_prob()`, the categories are the levels of the factor, including any levels with no observations, $a$ is set by the `prior` argument, and leave-one-out estimates are given by `loo = TRUE`.

### Several categorical variables

With two or more categorical variables, each combination of categories can be treated as a single category, and the methods above apply directly.
@fig-road-user-age shows the deaths cross-classified by road user and by age in five-year groups, giving 108 combinations ($6 \times 18$).
The joint probability of each combination is estimated by the proportion of deaths in that cell, and its surprisal probability is then computed from @eq-pi-categorical, with the cells in place of the categories.
The `interaction()` function combines the two variables into a single factor whose levels are the cells.

```{r}
#| label: road-user-age
#| code-fold: false

deaths <- road_deaths |>
  filter(!is.na(road_user), !is.na(age)) |>
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(
      age,
      breaks = c(seq(0, 85, 5), Inf),
      labels = c(paste0(seq(0, 80, 5), "-", seq(4, 84, 5)), "85+"),
      right = FALSE
    ),
    cell = interaction(road_user, age_group),
    s = surprisals(cell),
    p = surprisals_prob(cell)
  )
cells <- deaths |>
  count(road_user, age_group, s, p)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-road-user-age
#| dependson: road-user-age
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Australian road deaths from 1989 to 2025, by road user and age group.
#|   Each cell shows the number of deaths, and is coloured on a log scale.
#|   Grey cells have no deaths.
#| fig-height: 3

cells |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = road_user, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n, colour = n < 100), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(transform = "log10", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  guides(x = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  labs(x = "Age group (years)", y = NULL)
```

The driver deaths at young ages reflect licensing laws.
Learner drivers may drive under supervision from age 16 (15¾ in the ACT), and alone from 17 in most states and 18 in Victoria, so few drivers are younger than 16, and most of the driver deaths in the 15--19 group are of people aged 17 to 19.

The least probable cells are shown below.

```{r}
#| label: road-user-age-joint
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: road-user-age

cells |>
  arrange(p)
```

The least probable cells include drivers aged 0--4 and 5--9, very young motorcycle riders and pillion passengers, motorcycle riders aged 85 and over, and pillion passengers in their sixties.
The three cells with a single death are tied, so each has $p_i = 3/n$.
Neither drivers nor young children are unusual among road deaths; what is unusual is the combination.
The five drivers in the 0--4 group are all recorded as aged zero, so they are clearly recording errors.
At least some of the other young drivers or motorcycle riders are also likely to be recording errors.

The simplest model for several variables assumes that they are independent, so that $f(y_1, y_2) = f_1(y_1) f_2(y_2)$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the probability mass functions of the two variables.
The surprisal of an observation is then the sum of its surprisals on each variable separately, $s_i = -\log f_1(y_{i1}) - \log f_2(y_{i2})$.
The attribute value frequency (AVF) score of @Koufakou2007 is based on the same idea, averaging the frequencies of an observation's values instead of adding their surprisals.
Under independence, only the proportions of each variable separately need to be estimated, so the model works with any number of variables, but it can only find observations with rare values, not rare combinations of common values.
The columns `s_ind` and `p_ind` below give the surprisals and surprisal probabilities under independence.
The surprisal probabilities depend on the probabilities of all 108 cells, including those with no deaths, so these are passed to `surprisals_prob()` with the `prob` argument, in the order of the levels of the factor (with road user varying fastest).

```{r}
#| label: road-user-age-ind
#| code-fold: false
#| dependson: road-user-age-joint

f_user <- prop.table(table(deaths$road_user))
f_age <- prop.table(table(deaths$age_group))
cells <- deaths |>
  mutate(
    s_ind = surprisals(road_user) + surprisals(age_group),
    p_ind = surprisals_prob(cell, prob = c(outer(f_user, f_age)))
  ) |>
  count(road_user, age_group, s, p, s_ind, p_ind)
cells |>
  arrange(p_ind)
```

```{r}
#| label: road-user-age-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: [road-user-age-joint, road-user-age-ind]

get_cell <- function(user, age) {
  cells |> filter(road_user == user, age_group == age)
}
top_joint <- cells |> arrange(p) |> head(10)
top_ind <- cells |> arrange(p_ind) |> head(10)
young_drivers <- deaths |> filter(road_user == "Driver", age_group == "0-4")
# The prose describes the least probable cells under each model
stopifnot(
  nlevels(interaction(deaths$road_user, deaths$age_group)) == 108,
  nlevels(deaths$road_user) == 6,
  nlevels(deaths$age_group) == 18,
  all(
    c("0-4", "5-9") %in% top_joint$age_group[top_joint$road_user == "Driver"]
  ),
  get_cell("Driver", "0-4")$p < 0.001,
  get_cell("Driver", "5-9")$p < 0.001,
  all(
    top_joint$road_user %in%
      c("Driver", "Motorcycle rider", "Motorcycle pillion passenger")
  ),
  all(c("60-64", "65-69") %in% top_joint$age_group),
  sum(cells$n == 1) == 3,
  all(top_joint$p[1:3] == 3 / sum(cells$n)),
  all(top_joint$road_user == "Motorcycle rider" | top_joint$age_group != "85+"),
  "85+" %in% top_joint$age_group[top_joint$road_user == "Motorcycle rider"],
  NROW(young_drivers) == 5,
  all(young_drivers$age == 0),
  names(which.max(table(deaths$road_user))) == "Driver",
  names(which.min(table(deaths$road_user))) == "Motorcycle pillion passenger",
  get_cell("Driver", "0-4")$p_ind > 0.1,
  all(top_ind$road_user[1:9] == "Motorcycle pillion passenger"),
  top_ind$road_user[10] != "Motorcycle pillion passenger"
)
```

Drivers are the most common type of road user, and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * f_age["0-4"])`% of the deaths were of children aged 0--4, so under independence a driver aged 0--4 is unremarkable, with a surprisal probability of `r sprintf("%.2f", get_cell("Driver", "0-4")$p_ind)`.
The nine largest surprisals under independence all belong to motorcycle pillion passengers, the rarest type of road user, whatever their age.

The joint surprisal can be split into two parts,
$$
  s_i = -\log f_1(y_{i1}) - \log f(y_{i2} \mid y_{i1}),
$$
where $f(y_2 \mid y_1) = f(y_1, y_2)/f_1(y_1)$ is the conditional probability of the second variable given the first.
The second term is a **conditional surprisal**, measuring how surprising the age group is for that type of road user.
Independence replaces it by $-\log f_2(y_{i2})$, which ignores the road user category.
For drivers aged 0--4, the conditional surprisal is `r sprintf("%.1f", get_cell("Driver", "0-4")$s + log(f_user["Driver"]))`, whereas $-\log f_2(y_{i2})$ is only `r sprintf("%.1f", -log(f_age["0-4"]))`.

```{r}
#| label: road-sparsity
#| dependson: road-user-age
#| include: false

deaths7 <- deaths |>
  select(state, road_user, age_group, gender, crash_type, day_of_week, month) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()
combinations <- deaths7 |> count(across(everything()))
n_possible <- prod(sapply(deaths7, n_distinct))
n_unique <- sum(combinations$n == 1)
```

When there are more variables, the number of combinations grows multiplicatively, and most combinations have few or no observations.
For example, classifying the deaths by state, road user, age group, sex, crash type (single or multiple vehicle), day of the week and month gives `r scales::comma(n_possible)` possible combinations, many more than there are deaths.
Of the `r scales::comma(NROW(deaths7))` deaths with all seven variables recorded, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * n_unique / NROW(deaths7))`% are the only death with their combination of values.
These deaths all have the same estimated surprisal, $\log n$, and the same surprisal probability, `r sprintf("%.2f", n_unique / NROW(deaths7))`, so none of them is anomalous, and the model cannot distinguish between them.

Between independence and the full joint distribution are models in which each variable depends on only a few others.
Any joint distribution can be written as a product of conditional distributions,
$$
  f(y_1, \dots, y_m)
  = f_1(y_1) f(y_2 \mid y_1) f(y_3 \mid y_1, y_2) \cdots f(y_m \mid y_1, \dots, y_{m-1}),
$$
so the surprisal of an observation is a sum of conditional surprisals, one for each variable.
A **Chow--Liu tree**\ [@Chow1968] approximates the joint distribution by conditioning each variable on just one other variable, chosen to give the closest such approximation to the joint distribution.
More generally, a **Bayesian network** allows each variable to depend on a small set of other variables, and can be estimated using the **`bnlearn`** package\ [@Scutari2010].
Each conditional probability is then estimated from a two- or three-way table, most of whose cells contain enough observations, and the conditional surprisals show which variable makes an observation surprising, given the variables it depends on.

### Anomalous cells in a contingency table

A table of counts cross-classified by two categorical variables is called a **contingency table**.
For example, the contingency table below gives the deaths by state and road user.

```{r}
#| label: state-road-user-table
#| code-fold: false

state_user <- with(road_deaths, table(road_user, state))
state_user
```

Sometimes the question is not which observations are anomalous, but which cells of a contingency table have unusual counts.
As with the DDC algorithm (@sec-ddc), the anomalies are cells rather than observations, but here each cell is a count of observations rather than a single value.

Let $n_{jk}$ be the count in row $j$ and column $k$, with row totals $n_{j \cdot}$, column totals $n_{\cdot k}$, and $n$ observations in total.
If the two variables are independent, the expected count in each cell is $e_{jk} = n_{j \cdot}n_{\cdot k}/n$.
The **standardised residual** of a cell is
$$
  r_{jk} = \frac{n_{jk} - e_{jk}}{\sqrt{e_{jk}(1 - n_{j \cdot}/n)(1 - n_{\cdot k}/n)}},
$$
which has approximately a standard Normal distribution under independence, provided the expected counts are not too small.
As for the standardised residuals of a regression (@sec-residuals), each residual is divided by its standard deviation, so the residuals are $z$-scores (@sec-zscores) for the cell counts, and a cell with a large value of $|r_{jk}|$ is anomalous under the independence model.

The standardised residuals are returned by `chisq.test()`, and are shown in @fig-state-road-user.

```{r}
#| label: fig-state-road-user
#| code-fold: false
#| warning: false
#| dependson: state-road-user-table
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   Standardised residuals of Australian road deaths from 1989 to 2025, by state and road user, under an independence model.
#|   Red cells have more deaths than expected, and blue cells have fewer.
#| fig-height: 3

state_user_test <- chisq.test(state_user)
stdres <- as.data.frame(state_user_test$stdres, responseName = "r")
stdres |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = road_user, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", r)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "RdBu",
    limits = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(stdres$r)),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: state-road-user-check
#| include: false
#| dependson: fig-state-road-user

share <- prop.table(state_user, 2)
overall <- prop.table(rowSums(state_user))
r <- state_user_test$stdres
others <- colnames(share) != "NT"
# The prose describes these residuals and proportions
stopifnot(
  max(abs(r)) == r["Passenger", "NT"],
  length(r) == 48,
  sum(abs(r) > 2) == 28,
  sum(abs(r) > 3) == 16,
  round(r["Passenger", "NT"], 1) == 11.0,
  round(r["Driver", "NT"], 1) == -8.0,
  round(r["Motorcycle rider", "QLD"], 1) == 8.7,
  round(r["Pedestrian", "NSW"], 1) == 8.4,
  round(r["Pedestrian", "WA"], 1) == -8.1,
  share["Passenger", "NT"] > max(share["Passenger", others]),
  share["Driver", "NT"] < min(share["Driver", others]),
  sum(state_user_test$expected < 5) == 1,
  state_user_test$expected["Motorcycle pillion passenger", "ACT"] < 5
)
```

The Northern Territory stands out.
Passengers account for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share["Passenger", "NT"])`% of its road deaths, compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(share["Passenger", others]))`--`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(share["Passenger", others]))`% elsewhere, giving the largest residual in the table, and drivers account for only `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share["Driver", "NT"])`%, compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(share["Driver", others]))`--`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(share["Driver", others]))`% elsewhere.
Queensland has more motorcycle rider deaths than expected, New South Wales has more pedestrian deaths, and Western Australia has fewer pedestrian deaths.

Under independence, about 5% of the residuals would be larger than 2 in absolute value; here, `r english::words(sum(abs(r) > 2))` of the `r english::words(length(r))` residuals are, so the independence model clearly does not hold.
With `r scales::comma(sum(state_user))` deaths, even small differences in proportions give large residuals: pedestrians make up `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * share["Pedestrian", "NSW"])`% of the deaths in New South Wales and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * overall["Pedestrian"])`% of all deaths, yet the residual is `r sprintf("%.1f", r["Pedestrian", "NSW"])`.
So in a large table, the residuals are more useful for ranking the cells than for testing each one.
The Normal approximation is also poor for cells with small expected counts, such as the motorcycle pillion passengers in the ACT, whose expected count is `r sprintf("%.1f", state_user_test$expected["Motorcycle pillion passenger", "ACT"])`.

Looking at the cells one at a time does not show how whole states differ: the Northern Territory differs from the other states in several types of road user at once.
Correspondence analysis, described in the next section, compares whole rows and columns of a contingency table, and so finds states, or types of road user, that are anomalous.
